full_judgment:
2. The above miscellaneous case was for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and it was tiled by the present petitioners. 

 "Any land used as a homestead by its owner in the rural area shall be exempted from all legal processes, including seizure, distress, attachment or sale by any officer, court or any other authority and the owner of such land shall not be divested or dispossessed of the land or evicted therefrom by any means provided that nothing in this section shall apply to the acquisition of such home-stead under any law." 

 12. I have examined the written objection filed by the purchaser opposite party No.1 in the trial court carefully. In this written objection the purchaser nowhere has stated that he has been using the case land as his homestead. Though in this written objection purchaser-Opposite party No. 1 has stated that after purchasing the case land he has constructed one pucca but and a boundary wall on the case land by spending a total amount of Tk. 1,28,885.79 and has been possessing the same but he has not stated that he has been residing there i.e. in that hut. In the deposition of purchaser-opposite party No. 1 also there is nothing to the effect that he has been possessing the case land as his homestead. Rather, during cross-examination, this opposite party No. 1 has stated that he has got his paternal homestead which consists of 4 rooms and which is 3 kilometer off from the case land. Save and except the opposite party No. 1 himself no other man has been examined from his side. It should be mentioned here that this purchaser opposite party No. 1 neither in his written objection nor in his deposition has stated any such case that the case land is not agricultural land and as such this case for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not maintainable. Rather, in his written objection the purchaser opposite party No. I has stated that he has constructed one but within the case land and has been possessing the remaining of the case land through cultivation. However, both the courts below appear to have relied on some statements of the P.W. 1. This P.W. 1. during cross-examination, has stated that the opposite party No. 1 has one shop hut, a tube-well and a boundary wall within the case land and that after tiling of this case for pre-emption the opposite party No. 1 constructed those structures on the case land. However, this P.W. did not state at all that the purchaser-opposite party No. 1 has been using the case land as his homestead. So I find that there was no evidence at all before the learned courts below to hold that the purchaser-opposite party No. 1 has been using the case land as his homestead. The mere fact that the purchaser constructed some structures within the case land after his purchase does not attract section 6 of Land Reforms Ordinance 19S4 to invalidate a pre-emption proceeding under section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It appears that in view of the above referred statements of the P.W. 1 the learned appellate court has further observed that the case land is not agricultural land and as such this case for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not maintainable. This observation of the teamed appellate court also is erroneous. Because admittedly the structure on the case land was constructed after the impugned sale. There is no evidence at all on record to show that at the time of impugned sale the case land was not agricultural land. Rather the own statement of the purchaser-opposite party No. 1 in his written objection to the effect that he has been possessing the remaining portion of the case land through cultivation proves that at the time of his purchase the case land was agricultural land. The subsequent construction of any shop or other structure within the case land does not invalidate this case for pre-emption tiled under section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 14. In this case for pre-emption there is another point for determination, but none of the courts below has decided this point inspire of availability of sufficient materials/evidence before them. The purchaser Opposite Party No. 1 in his written statement has pleaded a clear and definite case that he has spent a total amount of Tk. 1,28,885.79 for constructing a hut and boundary wall etc. in the case land. At the time of argument before this revisional court the learned Advocate for the petitioner has pointed out that before the trial court the purchaser opposite party No. 1 himself prayed for assessment of the costs spent for the improvement of the case land by a commissioner and his prayer was allowed and the learned trial court appointed a competent person to assess the improvement cost on spot verification and accordingly the said Commissioner after holding enquiry, submitted report mentioning the improvement cost as Tk. 80,215.00 (Eighty thousand and two hundred fifteen). Against that report of the Commissioner the opposite party No. 1 did not file any objection, rather he accepted the same. Thereafter, as per direction of the court the petitioners deposited the said amount i.e. 80,215/- as improvement cost through challan and thereby accepted that improvement cost as correct. Order No. 28 dated 25.2.1995 and order No. 38 dated 10.4.1995 and also the other orders of the trial court record substantiate the above stated facts pointed out by the learned Advocate for the petitioners. It appears that the purchaser opposite party himself, which deposing before the learned trial court, admitted that he himself prayed for assessment of the improvement cost and the improvement cost which had been assessed by the Commissioner was correct and he did not file any objection against that report of the Commissioner regarding the improvement cost. During argument before this revisional Court also the purchaser opposite party respondent did not say anything as to the correctness of the improvement cost which was assessed by the Commissioner appointed by the court at his own initiative. However it appears that there are sufficient materials on record to give a decision as to the claim of improvement cost of the purchaser O.P. No. 1 by this revisional court without sending the case on remand to the trial court for the purpose of awarding improvement costs only. Where there are sufficient materials on records tor determining the improvement cost it will be unnecessary and also only time-consuming to send back the case on remand to the trial court for the purpose of determination and awarding the improvement cost only. In view of above facts and material on record I fix the improvement costs at Tk. 80215.00 (Eighty thousand and two hundred fifteen) which has already been deposited by the pre-emptor-petitioner in favour of pre-emptee Opposite Party No. 1.
